title: Wire Up Every Point
statement:
You get n distinct points on a grid, points[i] = [x, y]. A cable between two points costs their Manhattan distance, |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|, because cables run along the grid lines.

Lay cables so that every point is connected to every other one, directly or through other points. Return the smallest total cost. Cables only join at points; they never branch in the middle.

examples.why: Linking each point to its nearest neighbour gives two separate pairs for a total of 2. One more cable of length 9 is needed to join the pairs: 1 + 9 + 1.
Wiring in input order costs 10 + 8 = 18. The cheapest wiring is [0, 0]–[1, 1] (2) plus [1, 1]–[5, 5] (8).
A single point is already connected.

hints: The cheapest wiring never contains a loop: removing one cable of a loop keeps everything connected and only saves money. So you are looking for a tree over the points.
Grow a connected group one point at a time. Which point should join next, and through which cable?

Prim: keep, for every point outside the group, the cheapest cable to any point inside. Add the point with the smallest such cable, then update the others with their distance to the newcomer. With all pairs as possible edges, a plain O(n²) scan beats a heap.

explain.intuition:
Any connected wiring with a loop can drop one cable of the loop and stay connected, so the cheapest wiring is a tree: a minimum spanning tree (MST) of the complete graph where every pair of points is an edge.

The idea behind every MST algorithm is the cut rule: split the points into two groups any way you like; the cheapest cable crossing between the groups is safe to use. Some cable must cross the split, and swapping a pricier crossing cable for the cheapest one can only lower the cost. Prim's algorithm applies it to the split "points already wired" vs "the rest": repeatedly add the outside point with the cheapest cable into the group. Kruskal's algorithm applies it differently: sort all cables by length and take each one unless its two ends are already connected, checked with union-find.

Here every pair is an edge, so there are about n²/2 edges. Kruskal must sort them all: O(n² log n). Prim with a simple array of "cheapest cable into the group" needs no heap and no edge list: n rounds, each scanning n points, O(n²). On a dense graph that is the better choice.
steps: Keep best[i]: the cheapest cable from point i to the wired group. Start with best[0] = 0 and all others infinite.
Repeat n times: pick the unwired point u with the smallest best[u], mark it wired, and add best[u] to the total.
For every still-unwired point v, set best[v] = min(best[v], dist(u, v)).
pitfalls: Connecting every point to its nearest neighbour. That can leave separate islands, as in example 1.
In Kruskal, adding a cable whose ends are already connected. Without the union-find check you create a loop and pay for it.

solutions.title: Kruskal with union-find
solutions.idea: List every pair as an edge, sort by length, and take an edge whenever its ends are in different groups. Stop after n − 1 edges.

solutions.title: Prim with an array
solutions.idea: Grow the wired group one point at a time, always adding the outside point with the cheapest cable into the group. An array of cheapest cables replaces the heap.

followups: The points become 10⁵. Neither O(n²) approach fits. Which property of Manhattan distance lets you keep only a few candidate edges per point?
Some pairs already have a free cable between them. How do you adapt Kruskal?
